identity.title: Breeding the unbreedable: bottlenecks and genetic pathways to climate-resilient saffron (Crocus sativus L.).

content.abstract: Cultivated saffron (Crocus sativus L.) is a sterile autotriploid clone (2n = 3x = 24), propagated by corm division for roughly 3,600 years from a single auto-triploidisation event. Sequence-level polymorphism across the global crop is barely 4%, and no F2, recombinant inbred, QTL, or GWAS population has ever been produced, because triploid meiosis forecloses recombination-based breeding outright. This genetic standstill coincides with an accelerating production crisis: Kashmir has lost over 70% of its historical stigma yield, and global stigma yield has fallen by roughly 35% over recent decades. Methylation polymorphism across the World Saffron and Crocus Collection is eight-fold higher than sequence polymorphism, making epigenetic divergence the only substantial non-mutagenic source of heritable variation currently accessible. Heat, drought, cold, and Fusarium-driven disease converge on the florigen activation complex and the apocarotenoid pathway, defining a compact target set led by CsatSVP2, CsCCD2, and a defined NBS-LRR resistance-gene catalogue. Against the genomic infrastructure now available, including a fully phased 8.42 Gb triploid assembly, we evaluate the strategies open to this crop: epigenomic selection, clean-stock reform, induced mutagenesis, soma-clonal selection, wild-relative pre-breeding, and CRISPR/base/prime editing. Improvement is no longer limited mainly by a shortage of molecular targets or tools, but by a small number of translational bottlenecks, foremost the absence of any published whole-plant regeneration pipeline for edited tissue. We rank these bottlenecks by dependency and set out our own view of research priorities for the next five to fifteen years.
